Ibn Kathir notes that this very quality was how he was described in the previous Scriptures, quoting 7:157: "Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered, about whom they find written with them in the Tawrah and the Injīl — he commands them with good and forbids them from evil." And he adds that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained this way, unable to write even one line or one letter; he had scribes who would write down the revelation for him, or write letters from him to be sent to different places.

**"In that case, indeed, the followers of falsehood might have doubted."** Ibn Kathir: 'if you had been literate, some ignorant people would have doubted you. They would have said that you learned this from Books inherited from the Prophets which came before.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: had he been literate, there could have been a possibility of the disbelievers levelling the charge that he was repeating what he had read in the earlier Books, the Tawrah and Injīl, and that this was no fresh revelation sent down by way of prophethood.

Then comes the bitter proof of the point. **They said it anyway.** Ibn Kathir observes that they did indeed say it, even though they knew he was unlettered and could not read or write, quoting their words in 25:5: "Tales of the ancients, which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon" — and Allah's reply in 25:6: "Say: it has been sent down by Him who knows the secret of the heavens and the earth." So the doubt that ayah 48 says *would* have arisen if he were literate was manufactured regardless. This is exactly what the closing words of both ayah 47 and ayah 49 are getting at: the obstacle was never the evidence.

## A question the scholars raised: did he ﷺ later learn to write?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that some scholars tried to prove he was unlettered at first but that Allah later taught him how to read and write, citing in support a hadith about the incident at Hudaybiyah. When the agreement between the Prophet ﷺ and the disbelievers of Makkah was being written, the Muslims began it "From Muhammad, the slave of Allah and His Messenger." The Makkans objected: his being the Messenger of Allah was the real bone of contention — had they accepted him as such, there would have been no dispute at all — so they would not accept the words "and His Messenger" alongside his name. Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) had written the agreement, and when the Prophet ﷺ asked him to erase it he declined out of respect and reverence for him. So the Prophet ﷺ took the paper in his own hand, erased the words, and wrote "From Muhammad, son of ʿAbdullāh."

Because the act of writing is attributed to him in that narration, some concluded he knew how to write. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the correct position and three considerations against that conclusion:

1. **The idiom.** The act of writing was attributed to him in the narration as a colloquial expression. It is a fairly common idiom, spoken quite widely, that when someone has something written by a scribe, the writing is attributed to him even though he did not write it himself.
2. **The alternative possibility.** Allah may have made him write that bit miraculously on that particular occasion.
3. **The definition.** By writing just a few words one cannot be called literate; he would still remain unlettered.

And the decisive point of principle: it would be **no honour** for him to be labelled literate — rather, the honour lies in his being unlettered. That reframes the whole discussion. Illiteracy is a lack in an ordinary man; in this man it is the guarantee that what came through him did not come from him.

## Ayah 49: a Book that lives in chests

"Nay, but it is clear signs, preserved in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge." The word *bal* — "nay, but" — sweeps their accusation aside and replaces it with the truth about where this revelation actually resides.

Ibn Kathir explains: this Qur'an is clear signs which indicate the truth, commands, prohibitions and stories; it is memorised by the scholars for whom Allah makes it easy to memorise, recite and interpret. He connects this to 54:17: "And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy to understand and remember; then is there anyone who will remember?" The ease is itself part of the sign — the Book that no one could naturally have produced is a Book that ordinary people can carry, whole, inside them.

Ibn Kathir cites the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as saying that there has never been any Prophet who was not given that which would make people believe in him; what he himself was given was revelation which Allah revealed to him, and he hoped that he would have the most followers among them. Every prophet was given something by which people would believe; what this Prophet ﷺ was given was the revelation itself.

Then, from the hadith of ʿIyāḍ bin Ḥimār recorded in **Sahih Muslim**, Allah says: "I am testing you and testing others through you, revealing to you a Book which cannot be washed away by water, which you recite while you are asleep and while you are awake."

Ibn Kathir's commentary on that line is worth reading slowly. The meaning is that if the manuscript on which it is written were to be washed with water, there would be no need for that manuscript — because it is preserved in the hearts and is easy on the tongue, and it is controlling people's hearts and minds. It is miraculous in its wording and in its meanings. And he adds that in the previous Scriptures this Ummah was described as carrying their holy Books in their hearts.

Set that against ayah 48 and the two halves lock together. The Prophet ﷺ never wrote a line of it — and, as Ibn Kathir's comment shows, the survival of the revelation was never resting on the manuscript in the first place. The ink was never the point.

## From "disbelievers" to "wrongdoers"

The two ayat close almost identically, but not quite. Ayah 47 ends "none but **the disbelievers** (al-kāfirūn) reject Our signs"; ayah 49 ends "none but **the wrongdoers** (al-ẓālimūn) deny Our signs." Ibn Kathir's gloss on the second brings out what that word carries here: nobody denies it, or tries to undermine its status, or rejects it, except the wrongdoers — "the arrogant transgressors who know the truth but turn away from it."

That is a diagnosis, not an insult. On this reading the problem is not a shortage of information; it is knowing where the truth lies and turning from it anyway. Ibn Kathir seals the point with 10:96–97: "Truly those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe — even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment." When the will has already decided, additional evidence changes nothing. The one who covers his own eye will not be helped by a brighter sun.

## Living it

**Argue the way ayah 46 tells you to.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's guidance is concrete and hard: politeness against insolence, mildness against rage, dignified speech against uproar — and even when you would be justified in answering in kind, patience is better. These ayat then supply the confidence that makes such restraint possible: the case for the Qur'an does not need heat behind it.

**Know what you are affirming and what you are not.** Following the instruction recorded in Sahih Al-Bukhari, when reports from earlier scriptures reach you, neither believe nor reject them — say, "We believe in what is sent down to us and sent down to you." And remember that such narrations, where commentators quote them, are there to show a historical position; no ruling of halal or haram is built on them.

**Carry the Book where it is meant to be carried.** Ayah 49 does not say the Qur'an is in the pages of those given knowledge; it says it is in their **chests**. Ibn Kathir's whole explanation of the Book's preservation rests on that: it is kept in the hearts and made easy on the tongue, and 54:17 declares that Allah has made the Qur'an easy to remember — "then is there anyone who will remember?"

**Check your own resistance.** The passage's most searching line is that denial belongs to those "who know the truth but turn away from it." The honest question is not whether the proof is sufficient; it is whether some part of me would rather it were not.

passages.title: Demanding signs when the Book suffices
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer one objection. The idolaters of Makkah demanded that signs be sent down to confirm Muhammad ﷺ; the reply comes in three moves — signs belong to Allah alone, not to the Messenger (ayah 50); the Book already being recited to them is itself sufficient as a sign (ayah 51); and if they still refuse, the case rests with the only Witness whose testimony finally matters (ayah 52). Notice how the word "sufficient" threads through the passage: *Is it not sufficient for them…* and *Sufficient is Allah for a witness*. They asked for more; the answer is that what they already have is enough, and that Allah Himself is enough.

## The demand behind the demand (ayah 50)

Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters were stubbornly demanding signs: they wanted signs to show them that Muhammad ﷺ was indeed the Messenger of Allah, "just as Salih was given the sign of the she-camel." That comparison is the key to what they were asking for. They had in mind a sign of the same order as the one given to an earlier prophet, produced on request.

**"The signs are only with Allah."** The reply the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to give does not argue with them; it relocates the whole question. Ibn Kathir paraphrases it: the matter rests with Allah, and if He knew that they would be guided, He would respond to their request, "because it is very easy for Him to do that. Yet He knows that you are merely being stubborn and putting me to the test, so He will not respond to you."

Two things are worth pausing on here. First, the withholding is not from inability — Ibn Kathir is explicit that responding would be very easy for Him. Second, it is not arbitrary either; it is a judgement founded on His knowledge of what is actually in these hearts. They were not withholding belief for lack of evidence; they were being stubborn and putting the Messenger to the test.

Ibn Kathir supports this by citing Allah's words elsewhere: "And nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them. And We sent the she-camel to Thamud as a clear sign, but they did her wrong" (17:59). The very precedent they invoked — Salih's she-camel — is the precedent that answers them. The people of old were sent signs and denied them; Thamud were given the she-camel as a clear sign, and they wronged her. The spectacle they are asking for has been tried, and the record of it is not encouraging.

**"I am only a plain warner."** The second half of the reply defines the Prophet's ﷺ role precisely. Ibn Kathir: "I have been sent to you only as a warner to bring a clear warning; all I have to do is convey the Message of Allah to you." He is not a producer of wonders on demand, and he is not the one who opens hearts. Ibn Kathir underlines this with two further ayat: "He whom Allah guides, he is the rightly-guided; but he whom He sends astray, for him you will find no guide to lead him" (18:17), and "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills" (2:272).

There is real mercy in this for the Prophet ﷺ, and for anyone who carries the message after him. The duty is delivery, clearly and faithfully. The outcome is not the messenger's burden to carry.

## The sign they were standing inside (ayah 51)

Then comes the counter-question: "Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?"

Ibn Kathir says that here Allah shows how ignorant and foolish they were when they demanded a sign to prove that what Muhammad ﷺ had brought was true — because "He brought them a great Book which falsehood cannot reach, neither from before it or behind it, it was greater than all other miracles, for the most eloquent of men could not match it or produce ten Surahs, or even one Surah like it." They were asking for a sign while the greater sign was being recited to them, in words the most eloquent among them could not rival.

Ibn Kathir then spells out what makes it evidence: "is it not sufficient as a sign for them that We have sent down to you this great Book which tells them about what happened before their time, what will happen after they are gone, and passes judgement between them. Even though you are an unlettered man who can neither read nor write, and you have not mixed with any of the People of the Book. Yet you brought them news of what was said in the first Scriptures showing what is right in the matters that they dispute over, and bringing clear and obvious truth." He adds two supporting ayat: "Is it not a sign to them that the learned scholars of the Children of Israel knew it (to be true)?" (26:197) and "They say: 'Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?' Has there not come to them the proof of that which is in the former Scriptures?" (20:133).

**The unlettered messenger.** Ibn Kathir's argument turns partly on the Prophet ﷺ being *ummī* — unlettered, unable to read or write, and with no mixing with the People of the Book from whom he might have learned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this matters. It calls his unlettered state one of the clear miracles by which Allah proved his prophethood: forty years of his life were spent that way before the eyes of the people of Makkah, without his reading or writing anything, and without acquaintance with the People of the Book — indeed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there were no People of the Book living in Makkah. Then, suddenly, at the age of forty, speech began to flow from his mouth that was a miracle not only in its theme and meaning but in the pinnacle of its eloquence. Had he been literate, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, there could have been a foothold for doubt: the disbelievers could have alleged he was repeating what he had read in the Torah and the Injīl, and that this was no new revelation.

Once that is held in view, the force of the counter-question lands. The Makkans knew this man and had watched him for decades. The sign was not somewhere else waiting to be sent down.

**A question the scholars raised.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that some scholars tried to argue the Prophet ﷺ was unlettered at first but was later taught by Allah to read and write, citing a narration about the treaty of Hudaybiyah — in which, after the Makkans refused to let "and His Messenger" stand beside his name, the Prophet ﷺ took the paper in his own hand, erased the words, and wrote "From Muhammad, the son of ʿAbdullah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the correct position is that the writing was attributed to him in the narration as a common idiom: when someone has something written by a scribe, the writing is ordinarily ascribed to him even though he did not write it himself. Another possibility, it adds, is that Allah made him write that much miraculously on that occasion. And in any case, by writing just a few words a person cannot be called literate; he would still be unlettered. Its conclusion is a beautiful one: being labelled literate would not have been an honour for him — the honour lies in his being unlettered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also gives a useful reading rule in this connection. Narrations of the People of the Book that commentators quote in their tafsirs are reproduced to highlight their historical position; they cannot be used for determining what is permitted (*halāl*) and what is not permitted (*harām*).

## "Mercy and a reminder"

Ayah 51 closes: "Verily, herein is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe." Ibn Kathir opens both words. In this Qur'an there is mercy — "that is, explanation of the truth and removal of falsehood." That is a striking definition of mercy: to be shown what is actually true, and to have what is false lifted off you. And there is a reminder — "a reminder to the believers of the punishment that is to come to the disbelievers and sinners."

The ayah is careful about who benefits: "for a people who believe."

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no Prophet who was not given some miracles that would make the people believe in him. What I have been given is revelation which Allah reveals to me, and I hope that I will have the greatest number of followers on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim.

This is the passage's argument in the Prophet's ﷺ own words. Every prophet was given miracles of some kind; what he ﷺ was given is the revelation itself — and with it, the hope he expressed of having the greatest number of followers on the Day of Resurrection. The very sign the Makkans dismissed as insufficient is the one he ﷺ was given.

## The Witness who settles it (ayah 52)

When an argument reaches deadlock, the case goes to a witness. So the Prophet ﷺ is told: "Say: Sufficient is Allah for a witness between me and you."

Ibn Kathir renders the meaning: "He knows best the words of denial that you utter, and he knows what I am telling you about Him and that He has sent me. If I were telling lies about Him, He would have executed His vengeance upon me." He then quotes the warning of Sūrah al-Hāqqah: "And if he had forged a false saying concerning Us, We surely would have seized him by his right hand, and then We certainly would have cut off his aorta, and none of you could have withheld Us from (punishing) him" (69:44–47).

Follow the logic. If this man were inventing revelation and attributing it to Allah, Allah would have seized him — and no one could have prevented it. Ibn Kathir completes the thought in the Prophet's ﷺ voice: "But I am telling the truth in what I say to you about Him, so He has supported me with clear miracles and definitive evidence." Not being struck down, but supported, is itself part of the testimony.

**"He knows what is in the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir's comment is one line: "nothing is hidden from Him at all." We affirm this knowledge as an attribute belonging to Allah in the manner that befits Him, without likening it to the knowing of creatures and without emptying it of meaning. Its force here is the one Ibn Kathir himself draws: this Witness knows best the words of denial they utter, and knows equally that the Messenger is telling the truth about Him.

**"And those who believe in falsehood, and disbelieve in Allah — it is they who are the losers."** Read the ayah's own wording slowly and the reversal is hard to miss: belief is given to falsehood, and disbelief is directed at Allah.

Ibn Kathir says this loss will be realised on the Day of Resurrection: they will be punished for what they did and will get what they justly deserve for rejecting the truth and following falsehood, for disbelieving in the Messengers of Allah even when there was proof that they were telling the truth, and for worshipping false gods with no evidence — "Allah will punish them for all that, for He is All-Wise and All-Knowing."

That last pairing answers the whole passage. They wanted a sign; He is All-Knowing, and knew that they were merely being stubborn and putting the Messenger to the test. They may have read the withholding as inability; He is All-Wise, and sending a sign would have been very easy for Him.

## Living it

**Stop waiting for a sign that has already come.** The Makkans' error was not that they wanted evidence — it was that they demanded evidence while a great Book was being recited to them. A believer can repeat the mistake in a quieter key: waiting for a dream, a feeling, an extraordinary event, before taking the Book seriously. Ayah 51 asks a question that is still ours to answer: is it not sufficient?

**Sit with the Book as a sign, not just as a text.** Ibn Kathir's description is worth returning to — a Book that tells of what happened before their time, what will happen after they are gone, and passes judgement between them; brought by a man who could neither read nor write. Reading it with that in mind changes recitation from a routine into an encounter with the proof itself.

**Deliver, and leave the rest.** "I am only a plain warner." When we convey something true to family or friends and it does not land, ayah 50 gives us both our job and its limits: all that is required is to convey the message clearly. "Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills."

**Let Allah be enough as Witness.** Ayah 52 is the answer for anyone whose sincerity is doubted or whose motives are misread while doing what is right. The One from whom nothing in the heavens and the earth is hidden has already seen it. That is sufficient — and knowing it is sufficient is exactly what frees a person from having to win every argument.

passages.title: Challenging Allah to hasten the punishment
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer a taunt. The idolaters had begun challenging the Prophet ﷺ to hurry along the punishment he kept warning them about — and Allah replies not by defending the warning but by explaining the delay, and then by describing, in exact detail, the very thing they were asking for. What holds ayat 53–55 together is a single movement: **the demand (53), the answer that it will undoubtedly come (54), and the scene of its arrival (55).**

## The taunt behind the words

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on these ayat by naming what is really happening: "Allah tells us of the ignorance of the idolators and how they asked for the punishment of Allah to be hastened so that it would befall them quickly."

That word — *ignorance* — is the key to the whole passage. The demand is not the question of someone weighing evidence. It is the swagger of someone who has decided in advance that nothing is coming, and who therefore treats the warning as a joke he can call the teller's bluff on.

Ibn Kathir shows just how far that swagger went by placing beside our ayah a line from Sūrat al-Anfāl, where such people prayed:

> "O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment." (8:32)

Read that slowly. They did not ask for guidance if it was the truth. They asked for *stones*. A man who genuinely suspects the message might be true and still prays for stones has not made an intellectual error — he has made a moral one. This is the mentality the Qur'an is answering in ayah 53.

## "Were it not for an appointed term"

Ayah 53 opens:

> **وَيَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِالْعَذَابِ**
> "They challenge you ˹O Prophet˺ to hasten the punishment."

Notice who the demand is aimed at. It is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ personally — as though the punishment were his to release, and he were the one holding it back. The jeering had a target, and the target was him.

Then comes the answer:

> **وَلَوْلَا أَجَلٌ مُسَمًّى لَجَاءَهُمُ الْعَذَابُ**
> "...and had it not been for a term appointed, the torment would certainly have come to them."

Ibn Kathir spells out what that appointed term is: "Were it not for the fact that Allah has decreed that the punishment should be delayed until the Day of Resurrection, the torment would have come upon them quickly as they demanded."

Notice what this does to their taunt. They read the silence of the sky as proof that there was nothing behind the warning. The ayah tells them the silence is proof of something else entirely — that a term has already been appointed, and the reason nothing has fallen on them is not that the threat was empty but that the appointment has not yet arrived. The very stillness they were gloating over was the restraint of the One they were mocking.

There is a mercy folded into this that they could not see. Every hour of that delay was an hour in which they could have turned back.

## "Suddenly, while they perceive not"

Ayah 53 does not end with the delay. It closes:

> **وَلَيَأْتِيَنَّهُمْ بَغْتَةً وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ**
> "And surely, it will come upon them suddenly while they perceive not."

Two things are promised here, and they belong together. It will come *suddenly* — and it will come while they are *not perceiving it*. The mockers wanted the punishment on a schedule they could watch. What they are told is that it will arrive without their seeing it coming at all — which is the exact opposite of what they asked for, and far worse.

## Ayah 54: "it will undoubtedly befall them"

Ayah 54 repeats their demand almost word for word: **يَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِالْعَذَابِ** — "They urge you to hasten the punishment."

The demand is stated twice in two consecutive ayat, and each time the reply is different. The first time, the reply explains the *delay*. The second time, the reply removes any comfort they might have drawn from that delay:

> **وَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمُحِيطَةٌ بِالْكَافِرِينَ**
> "And verily, Hell, of a surety, will encompass the disbelievers."

Ibn Kathir takes the two lines together and glosses them in one short, heavy sentence: "they ask you to hasten on the punishment, but it will undoubtedly befall them."

That is the whole answer to "hasten it." They are treating the punishment as something that may or may not exist, a bluff to be called. The ayah does not argue with them about whether it exists. It simply states that it will encompass them — and Ibn Kathir's word for that is *undoubtedly*. The thing they are daring to arrive is not in question. Only its timing is, and its timing is not theirs to set.

## Ayah 55: covered from above and beneath

Ayah 55 opens the door and shows them the room they were asking to be let into:

> **يَوْمَ يَغْشَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ وَمِنْ تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِمْ**
> "On the Day when the torment shall cover them from above them and from beneath their feet..."

The image is not of a blow struck from one direction. It is of being *covered* — from above, and from beneath the feet. Ibn Kathir gathers three other passages that draw the same picture, and reading them together is the point:

- "Theirs will be a bed of Hell, and over them coverings (of Hell-fire)." (7:41) — a bed beneath, a covering above. The two most ordinary comforts of a human being, turned into the instrument.
- "They shall have coverings of Fire, above them and coverings (of Fire) beneath them." (39:16)
- "If only those who disbelieved knew (the time) when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces, nor from their backs." (21:39) — the hands that would shield the face cannot, and behind the back there is no safety either.

Ibn Kathir then draws the conclusion himself: **"The Fire will cover them from all sides, which is more effective as a physical punishment."**

There is a grim logic in that last phrase — *more effective as a physical punishment*. A pain you can turn away from is survivable, because the body always keeps one direction of hope: a way to flinch, a way to shield. Covering from every side removes that. The horror here is not only the heat; it is that there is nowhere else to be.

## "Taste what you used to do"

The ayah does not stop at the physical. It ends:

> **وَيَقُولُ ذُوقُوا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ**
> "and it will be said: 'Taste what you used to do.'"

Ibn Kathir identifies exactly what this line is doing, and it is one of the most illuminating notes in the whole passage: **"This is a threat and a rebuke, which is a form of psychological punishment."**

So there are two punishments running at once in ayah 55, and Ibn Kathir names them as two. The Fire that covers them from above and below he calls *physical* punishment. The words spoken to them he calls *psychological* punishment — the humiliation of being told, at that very moment, why this is happening. Ibn Kathir supports the point with two further scenes:

- "The Day they will be dragged on their faces into the Fire (it will be said to them): 'Taste you the touch of Hell!' Verily, We have created all things with a measurement." (54:48–49)
- "The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing. This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic or do you not see? Enter you therein, and whether you are patient of it or impatient of it, it is all the same. You are only being requited for what you used to do." (52:13–16)

Read that second passage against ours and you can hear the echo of the taunt. *This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see?* Their own denial is handed back to them. They had asked for it; now it is delivered, and the delivery comes with the reminder that they placed the order.

And note the wording of the rebuke in our ayah. Not "taste the recompense of your deeds" but **"taste what you used to do"** — as though the deeds themselves were the substance now being tasted. The same note sounds in 52:16: *You are only being requited for what you used to do.* They spent a lifetime discussing the Fire as a theory. Now they are told to taste it.

## What this passage asks of us

The passage is aimed at scoffers, but it lands on anyone who has ever mistaken a delay for a dismissal.

**Do not read Allah's patience as Allah's absence.** The clearest lesson of ayah 53 is that nothing arriving is not the same as nothing coming. There is an appointed term, and Ibn Kathir tells us the appointment is the Day of Resurrection. The people most at risk are the ones who have concluded from a quiet sky that no one is watching.

**Do not ask for what you cannot bear.** The taunt of 8:32 quoted by Ibn Kathir — "rain down stones on us" — is the ancestor of every reckless dare thrown at heaven. Ibn Kathir calls the whole attitude *ignorance*, not courage. Better by far to ask for the mercy we actually need than to test a power we could not survive.

**Take the mercy in the delay.** Every day the appointed term has not arrived is a day still open for repentance. That is what the mockers wasted, and it is the same commodity we are all spending.

**And take heart if you are the one being mocked.** Ayah 53 puts the Prophet ﷺ on the receiving end of the jeering, and Allah's response to him is not a miracle to silence them but an explanation of the timing — a reassurance that the delay is His decree, not His neglect. Anyone carrying a truth that people laugh at is being taught here how to hold it: patiently, without needing the last word today, knowing that the term has already been appointed.

passages.title: Emigrate for faith; every soul tastes death
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are Allah's practical answer to everything the surah has been describing: hostility, rejection of His oneness and of the Prophet's ﷺ message, and obstacles thrown in the path of the truth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly — from the opening of the surah until now we have heard about the pressure believers were under; here we are shown the way out of it, and its name is *hijrah*, migration: to leave the home and land where you are forced to speak and act against the truth. What holds ayat 56–60 together is that ayah 56 issues the call, and ayat 57–60 dismantle, one by one, the two fears that keep a person from answering it.

## The moment behind the words

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 56 against a real scene. When life in Makkah became unbearable for the believers — weak, few, oppressed — they left for Ethiopia, where at last they could practise their religion. He says the Muslims found Ethiopia the best of hosts: its king, the Negus, Ashamah — may Allah have mercy on him — gave them refuge, helped them, supported them and honoured them in his land. Later the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Companions who remained migrated to Al-Madinah, which had been called Yathrib; may Allah protect it.

So this is not an abstract exhortation. It is addressed to people packing what they can carry and walking away from everything they own.

## Ayah 56: "My servants… My earth"

Notice how Allah opens: **يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا** — "O My servants who believe." He does not say "O you people." He claims them as His own before He asks anything of them. And He does not say "the earth is spacious"; He says **أَرْضِي** — *My* earth. Ibn Kathir speaks of migrating "to the spacious earth of Allah." The land you are being driven out of is not the property of those driving you out. Every horizon you might flee toward already belongs to your Master.

**إِنَّ أَرْضِي وَاسِعَةٌ** — "Certainly, spacious is My earth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the argument out: Allah has made it clear that His land is very vast, so no one may plead as an excuse that he could not affirm Allah's oneness or worship Him because the disbelievers held power in a particular city or country. The excuse is closed off before it is spoken. If you are forced into disbelief and sin where you are, look for a place where you can live by Allah's commands — and, Maʿārif adds, persuade others to do the same. *That is what hijrah is all about.*

Then the command: **فَإِيَّايَ فَاعْبُدُونِ**. Maʿārif renders it "So, Me alone you worship." The instruction is not simply to worship, but to worship Him alone — and that, for Ibn Kathir, is the whole purpose of the move: Allah commands His believing servants to migrate to a land where they can establish Islam **by declaring Allah to be One and worshipping Him as He has commanded**. The point of moving is not comfort. It is that the worship of Allah alone should be possible again.

## Ayah 57: the first fear — "they will kill me on the road"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies two risks that predictably hold a person back from migrating. The first is the risk to his life: his adversaries may take up arms to stop him leaving, and even once he is away there is the danger of being caught on the road. Two threats to his life, going and gone.

The answer comes in the very next ayah: **كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَائِقَةُ الْمَوْتِ** — "Every soul will taste death." No one escapes death anywhere, in any situation. So, says Maʿārif, fear of death should not be a Muslim's trait, because whatever defences he arranges for himself, death will still overcome him — and it is part of a believer's faith that death cannot come before the time Allah has determined. Fear of dying, therefore, has no business deciding whether you stay somewhere or leave it.

Ibn Kathir gives the same verse the same work: *wherever you are, death will catch up with you, so always obey Allah and be where Allah commands you to be, for this is better for you.* Death is inevitable and there is no escape from it — and then comes **ثُمَّ إِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ**, "then to Us you will be returned." Whoever was obedient to Him will have the best reward.

Read the two halves together and the calculation flips. Staying does not buy you safety; it only changes where you happen to be standing when the appointed moment arrives. The one thing genuinely at stake is what you are found doing. And Maʿārif adds the sweetener: if death comes while you are carrying out a command of Allah, it brings eternal blessing and comfort in the Hereafter — which is exactly what the next two ayat describe.

## Ayat 58–59: what waits on the other side

**وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ** — Ibn Kathir's rendering is "to them We shall surely give lofty dwellings in Paradise"; Maʿārif's is "We shall accommodate them in mansions of the Paradise." Either way this is a promise, not a possibility — and against a promise like that, the losses of migration are being priced honestly.

**غُرَفًا** — Ibn Kathir renders these as *lofty dwellings*, high chambers in Paradise; Maʿārif calls them mansions. Beneath them rivers flow, and Ibn Kathir specifies the kinds: water, wine, honey and milk — and these are rivers the dwellers **can direct and cause to flow wherever they wish**. That is a striking detail. The one who lost his house, his fields and his shop, and could not so much as choose which street to walk down without harassment, is given a home where even the rivers go where he wants.

**خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا** — "to live therein forever," which Ibn Kathir explains as: they will remain there forever, *never wanting to leave*. Permanence without restlessness. The migrant's life is one long departure; this is the end of departures.

**نِعْمَ أَجْرُ الْعَامِلِينَ** — "Excellent is the reward for the workers." Ibn Kathir: these rooms will be a blessed reward for the good deeds of the believers. Not a windfall — wages, for work done.

### Who the "workers" are (ayah 59)

Ayah 59 names the two qualities that earn it, and Ibn Kathir defines both concretely.

**الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا** — "those who are patient": patient *in adhering to their religion*, who migrated for the sake of Allah and fought the enemy, leaving behind their families and relatives to seek Allah's Face, hoping for what is with Him and believing His promise. So *sabr* — patience — is not passive endurance of a bad mood here. It is the sustained refusal to trade your religion away, at the cost of home and kin, with nothing held in hand but a promise you trust.

**وَعَلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ** — "and put their trust in their Lord." Ibn Kathir: *in all their affairs, spiritual and worldly alike.* Tawakkul — reliance on Allah — is not a religious mode you switch into for prayer and switch out of for rent and work. In a passage about emigration, that breadth is the whole point.

### From the Sunnah

Commenting on these lofty chambers, Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim — may Allah have mercy on him — from Abu Muʿāniq al-Ashʿarī, that Abu Malik al-Ashʿarī told him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "In Paradise there are rooms whose outside can be seen from the inside, and their inside can be seen from the outside; Allah has prepared them for those who feed others, who speak well, who pray and fast continually, and who stand in prayer at night while people are asleep."

Look at the four keys handed out here: feeding people, good speech, steady prayer and fasting, and the night prayer nobody sees. Three are quiet and one is invisible. The rooms are transparent inside and out — nothing hidden in them — and they are earned by deeds whose sincerity is likewise hidden from everyone but Allah.

## Ayat 59–60: the second fear — "how will I eat?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the second risk of migration with real-world exactness. At home a person's living is arranged: employment, trade, cultivation, inherited land. Migration leaves all of it behind. *So how will he manage sustenance in a strange place?*

The answer, Maʿārif says, is given in the verses that follow, and it works by exposing a hidden mistake: you regard your worldly possessions and arrangements as the *cause* of your sustenance — but who gave you all this? It is your mistake to think you arranged it all on your own. Without the help and will of Allah nothing can be procured. If He wills, a person receives unlimited sustenance with no visible means at all; if He does not will it, a person gets nothing despite every visible means in place. This is why *tawakkul* in ayah 59 sits directly before the argument in ayah 60 — trust is not a feeling here, it is the correct reading of how provision actually works.

**وَكَأَيِّنْ مِنْ دَابَّةٍ لَا تَحْمِلُ رِزْقَهَا** — "How many a moving creature carries not its own provision!" Ibn Kathir explains: it does not have the ability to gather its provision and save it for tomorrow. Maʿārif fills in the picture from observation: countless animals neither collect nor store their sustenance, nor even worry about collecting it, yet Allah provides for them daily by His grace. The exceptions prove how rare storing is — ants and rats store (ants do not come out of their holes in winter, so they gather in summer), and among the birds the crow is the one that collects food in its nest, then forgets it. Maʿārif also mentions a hadith — without naming the collection it comes from — that the birds set off from their nests at dawn hungry and return in the evening satisfied; and so it goes throughout their lifetime.

**اللَّهُ يَرْزُقُهَا وَإِيَّاكُمْ** — "Allah provides for it *and for you*." The little word "and for you" is where the argument lands on the reader. Ibn Kathir: Allah allots the creature its provision even though it is weak, and makes it easy for it; He sends provision to every creature in the appropriate manner — even the ants in the depths of the earth, the birds in the air, and the fish in the sea. He brings in Allah's word elsewhere: *"And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah. And He knows its dwelling place and its deposit. All is in a Clear Book"* (Hud 11:6).

If provision reaches a creature that cannot plan, cannot store and cannot even conceive of tomorrow, then leaving a city does not cut you off from your Lord's giving. Ibn Kathir makes the point directly: provision is not limited to one place but is given to all His creatures no matter where they are — and in fact when the Muhajirin migrated their provision became **greater and better than before**, because after a short time they became rulers in the land, in all regions. The people who walked out with nothing were not impoverished by obedience.

## "And He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower"

The passage closes on two of Allah's names, and their placement is deliberate. Ibn Kathir explains **وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ**: He hears all that His servants say, and He knows their every movement.

Set that against the passage. Every anxiety here is spoken quietly or not spoken at all: *what if they kill me on the road, what if my children go hungry in a strange country.* The One who is asking you to go is As-Samīʿ — He hears all that His servants say — and Al-ʿAlīm — He knows their every movement, the journey included, and where each creature's provision is stored.

## Living it

- **Weigh a decision by what it costs your religion, not only by what it costs your comfort.** Ayah 56 assumes a believer may have to move for the sake of worship, and refuses "I couldn't practise where I was" as an excuse.
- **Do not let fear of death steer your choices.** Ayah 57's logic, in Maʿārif's words, is that death overtakes you regardless, and cannot come before the time Allah has determined.
- **Do not let fear of poverty steer them either.** Ayah 60 sends you to look at animals that cannot store food for tomorrow and are fed anyway.
- **Take the means, and know their source.** The passage never tells anyone to stop working; it tells you not to mistake your arrangements for the thing that actually feeds you.
- **Aim at the chambers.** The report cited by Ibn Kathir gives the plainest programme available: feed people, speak well, keep up prayer and fasting, and stand in prayer at night while people are asleep.

passages.title: They admit Allah creates yet still turn away
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat put a single question to the idolaters of Makkah — *who made all this, and who keeps it running?* — and then let their own answer convict them. They admit that Allah alone creates, controls and provides; and then they go on directing their worship and their trust somewhere else. What holds the passage together is that one movement: from an admission they cannot escape, to the behaviour that contradicts it.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these ayat in the flow of what came just before. The subject is hijrah — migration, leaving one place for another for the sake of one's religion. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies **worry about sustenance** as "the second impediment in the way of hijrah": if I leave my town, my trade, my land — what will I eat?

That fear, it says, "is based on wrong assumptions. Provision of sustenance is not in the hands of its resources, but it is a direct gift of Allah Taʿālā. It was He who had provided the sustenance in the first place, and it is He who would provide it at the second place. Therefore, this second assumed apprehension should also not come in the way of hijrah."

So ayat 61–63 are not an abstract theological detour. They are the answer to a frightened man's calculation. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this theme, beginning at ayah 61, continues "until the end of the rukūʿ" — the rukūʿ being one of the traditional sections the Qur'an is divided into for reading. This is one sustained argument, not three separate remarks.

## Ayah 61 — the admission they cannot avoid

*"And if you were to ask them: 'Who has created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?' They will surely reply: 'Allah.' How then are they deviating?"*

Notice the shape of it. Allah does not open by telling the Prophet ﷺ to assert something. He tells him to **ask a question** — and the Qur'an is so certain of the reply that it supplies it in advance: *they will surely reply, "Allah."*

Ibn Kathir sets out exactly what these idolaters conceded. They "recognized that He was the sole creator of the heavens and earth, the sun and the moon, alternating the night and day. They acknowledged that He was the Creator Who provided for His servants and decreed how long they should live." The problem was never that they had no idea who made the world. They knew, and said so.

Then comes the sting: *"How then are they deviating?"* Not *why do they not know* — but how, knowing this, do they still turn away?

**The logic Ibn Kathir draws out** is the heart of the passage: "Allah stated that He has alone created everything, and that He alone is controlling them – if this is how it is, then why worship anyone else? Why put one's trust in anyone else? Since dominion is His Alone, then let worship be for Him Alone."

Ibn Kathir then observes that this is a standard Qur'anic method: "Allah often establishes His divinity by referring to their acknowledgement of His Unique Lordship, because the idolators used to acknowledge His Lordship." In other words, the Qur'an argues from what its opponents already grant. They had conceded that He alone creates, owns and provides — His Lordship. What follows from that is that He alone deserves worship. The argument is simply a demand for consistency.

**The talbiyah detail.** Ibn Kathir offers one striking piece of evidence that they really did acknowledge His Lordship. In their talbiyah — the pilgrim's call of response, said during Hajj and ʿUmrah — they would say: "At Your service, You have no partner, *except the partner that You have, and You possess him and whatever he has.*"

Read that twice. In the very sentence where they deny Allah a partner, they insert one — and even then they cannot help admitting that this so-called partner is himself owned by Allah, along with everything he has. Their own devotional formula concedes the point mid-breath. That is precisely the condition ayah 61 exposes: the truth is on their tongues, and they still turn away from it.

## Ayah 62 — who decides who has more

*"Allah expands the provision for whom He wills of His servants, and straitens it for whom (He wills). Verily, Allah is the All-Knower of everything."*

Provision is expanded for some and restricted for others, and both are Allah's doing — not an accident of circumstance.

Ibn Kathir explains that this too was part of what the idolaters conceded: that Allah "made them and their provision different, so that some were rich and some were poor." And then he adds the point that turns the ayah from a statement of power into a source of peace: **"He knew best what was suitable for each of them, who deserved to be rich and who deserved to be poor."**

This is why the ayah closes with *"Allah is the All-Knower of everything."* The difference between one servant's portion and another's is not indifference and not arbitrariness. It issues from complete knowledge — of what is suitable for each person, one by one.

Placed where it is, ayah 62 does exact work on the fear that stalled the hijrah. If the One who expands and restricts provision is Allah, then the question "will I still be provided for if I leave?" has been aimed at the wrong address. Your provision was never in your town's hands to give — and it is therefore never in your town's hands to withhold.

## Ayah 63 — rain, dead earth, and a command to say thank you

*"And if you were to ask them: 'Who sends down water from the sky, and gives life therewith to the earth after its death?' They will surely reply: 'Allah.' Say: 'All the praises and thanks be to Allah!' Nay, most of them have no sense."*

The question of ayah 61 is now repeated in a lower, closer register. The first was cosmic — heavens, earth, sun, moon. This one is agricultural: the rain, and the green that comes up out of ground that had been dead. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pairs the questions exactly this way: who created the earth and the skies, who controls the movement of the sun and the moon, "who brings in the rain, and who makes the vegetation grow" — and on every one of them, "even they will admit that it is all controlled and done by One entity, that is Allah Taʿālā."

And rain is the perfect illustration of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's central point about sustenance: it "is not in the hands of its resources, but it is a direct gift of Allah Taʿālā."

**Then the response is prescribed.** After the admission is extracted, Allah does not tell the Prophet ﷺ to argue further. He tells him: *"Say: All the praises and thanks be to Allah!"* They said "Allah" and walked away; the believer says "Allah" and follows it with praise.

**"Nay, most of them have no sense."** The closing verdict is not that they lack information — they have just supplied the correct information themselves. What they lack is the sense to act on what they know, to let a conclusion travel from the tongue to the life. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the next move in the argument: they are to be asked "why do they then worship any other than Allah and regard it as their mentor."

## Living it

**Fix the address of your fear.** The passage speaks to people weighing a move that would cost them everything they earned from. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary is the practical core: He who provided for you in the first place is the same One who will provide in the second place. Means are real, and you work them — but they are not the source. Wherever obedience to Allah looks expensive, ayah 62 is the answer to the arithmetic.

**Audit your own contradiction.** The idolaters' failure was not in what they were willing to state about the Creator; it was in the gap between that and their conduct. Ibn Kathir asks two questions of them, and both land on us: *why worship anyone else? why put one's trust in anyone else?* A Muslim who says "Allah is my provider" and then places his real hope in an employer, a market, or a passport is standing nearer to the talbiyah of Makkah than he would like.

**Let the answer end in praise.** Ayah 63 does not leave recognition as a thought. It converts it into something said out loud: *all the praises and thanks be to Allah.* That is the difference the ayah is drawing between two kinds of people who give the same correct answer.

## The rulings Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attaches here

Because these ayat dissolve the excuse of livelihood, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān uses the occasion to set out when hijrah is actually obligatory. (It notes that the meaning, definition and blessings of hijrah were covered earlier, under Sūrah an-Nisāʾ 4:97–100, and that it is adding here an aspect omitted there.)

**How it was at the start.** When the Prophet ﷺ migrated from Makkah under instructions from Allah, and in turn instructed the Muslims to do the same provided they had the means, migration was obligatory for all Muslims. No man or woman was exempt; the only exemption was for those who did not have the means to migrate.

More than that, it was then "regarded as a sign of being Muslim" — one who did not migrate despite having the means "was not considered a Muslim, and was treated like an infidel," a point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces to Sūrah an-Nisāʾ 4:89, *"unless they migrate in the way of Allah."* It compares the position of hijrah in those days to professing the kalimah, *lā ilāha illā Allāh*: as a person is accepted into Islam only after reciting it, so migration was then required of anyone who had the means. And just as those who could not speak were exempt from pronouncing the kalimah, those without means were exempt from the journey — the exception in 4:98, *"except the oppressed."* Those who stayed in Makkah with the means to leave were warned severely in 4:97, where the angels ask, *"Was not the earth of Allah wide enough that you might have sought refuge in it?"*

**How it changed.** After the victory of Makkah the obligatory command for hijrah was withdrawn, because Makkah itself had turned into a house of Islam. The Prophet ﷺ issued the order *lā hijrata baʿd al-fatḥ* — that after the victory of Makkah there is no need to migrate from there. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that both the original command and its withdrawal are established from categorical statements of the Qur'an and Sunnah.

**The rulings the jurists derived from this:**

- If a person is not free to hold on to Islam in a city or country, and is constrained to act against its teachings or to follow the rites of disbelief, migration becomes obligatory upon him — to a place where he can follow and practise the teachings of Islam — **provided he has the means to do so**. If he has no means to travel, or there is no place available where he could fulfil his religious obligations, he is "excused" in the technical religious sense.
- If there is freedom of action to follow one's religion in a non-Muslim country, migration from there "is still preferable, though not compulsory or obligatory." And the trigger is not the label of the country: migration becomes obligatory from a country "where the commandments of Allah are flouted openly, no matter even if it is called Islamic on the basis of its Muslim rulers."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar adopted this ruling in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*, and that it does not conflict with Ḥanafī principles. It further cites a narration in the *Musnad* of Aḥmad, on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Yaḥyā, the client of Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, that the Prophet ﷺ said: **"All cities belong to Allah, and all the people are His servants. Therefore, wherever you find goodness you live there."**

It closes with two of the early authorities. Ibn Jarīr reported with his own chain of narrators that Sayyidnā Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: *leave that city where sins and obscenity are common.* And the Imam of Tafsīr, ʿAṭāʾ, said: *run away from the city where you are forced to commit sins.*

Read back against ayat 61–63, the connection is plain. What makes such a departure thinkable is knowing who actually sends the rain — that "all cities belong to Allah," and so does everything that grows in them.

passages.title: Sincerity at sea, forgotten on dry land
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat diagnose a single disease and name its cure. People who already admit that Allah alone created and controls everything still hand over part of their worship to others — and the reason, Allah says, is that they are lost in a life that is only amusement and play, and oblivious to the life that lasts forever. The passage moves in one arc: first the diagnosis, then an unforgettable illustration of it — the man who prays with perfect sincerity in a ship caught in a storm and forgets Allah the moment his feet touch dry sand — and finally the verdict.

## The question these ayat answer

To feel the force of this passage you have to hear the question it is answering. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets it out. In the ayat just before, Allah has pointed out that if the disbelievers are asked about the creation of the earth and the skies, the solar system, the water cycle and its effect on the growth of vegetation, they reply that all of it is created and controlled by Allah. They did not believe that anyone else had any involvement in creating or controlling any of it. Yet in their worship they still associated idols with Allah. Ayah 63 closes with the reason: *"Most of them do not understand."*

That raises an obvious objection, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises it honestly: after all, these were not insane people but intelligent and sensible ones. They performed many important and skilful jobs. So how had they lost their balance of mind?

The answer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is given in the first of these three ayat. They are not stupid. They are **lost in the love of the material attractions of this world** — attractions that are mortal and will soon disappear — and totally oblivious of the life of the Hereafter, which will last forever. That is why their intelligence fails them precisely where it matters most.

## A game that ends, and the life that does not

**"This worldly life is no more than play and amusement."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly what this comparison is meant to do. Amusements are finished and gone after a while and do not leave behind any objective or lasting impact — and the attractions of this world, it says, are similar in nature. Not that they are unreal while they last, but that they finish, and when they finish nothing of substance remains in your hands.

Ibn Kathir sums up this half of the ayah in a line: Allah is telling us **how insignificant and transient this world is, and how it will soon end.** All that it is, is amusement and play.

Then comes the contrast:

**وَإِنَّ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلۡـَٔاخِرَةَ لَهِىَ ٱلۡحَيَوَانُ** — Ibn Kathir renders it: *"Verily, the home of the Hereafter — that is the life indeed."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *"the Last Abode is the real life indeed."*

The word Allah uses here is *al-ḥayawān*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, citing Qurtubi, that *al-ḥayawān* is used here in the sense of *ḥayāh*, life. And Ibn Kathir gives the sense of what that life is: **the true, everlasting life that will never end, but will continue forever and ever.**

Put the two halves side by side and the ayah is making a claim about which of the two is more real. What is being lived now is amusement and play. What comes next is the life indeed.

**"If they but knew."** Ibn Kathir's gloss on this closing phrase is beautifully practical: it means that *they would prefer that which will last over that which will pass away.* That is his definition of knowing. Not information — preference. Real knowledge of the Hereafter shows up as a changed set of choices. A person who genuinely knows a game is a game does not sell the house to keep playing it.

## The ship: sincerity that lasts only as long as the fear

Ibn Kathir marks the turn himself. After that gloss, he says, Allah tells us that **at times of calamity the idolaters call upon Him alone, with no partner or associate — so why do they not do that all the time?** That question is the hinge of the whole passage.

**"And when they embark on a ship, they invoke Allah, making their faith pure for Him only."**

On that deck, at that moment, their worship is pure — for Him only. No idol is named. No intermediary is invoked. The very people who spend their lives dividing their devotion suddenly call on Allah alone, because the water has stripped away everything else they were leaning on.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights how surprising this is. Despite believing that Allah is unique and solitary in His creation, they associate idols with Him ignorantly. And yet whenever they are hit by some calamity, they have the **firm belief** that none of their idols has the power to take them out of it. They know well that it is only Allah who can remove the calamity, and that none of their idols could do anything. Their crisis exposes what they actually believed all along. Being totally helpless at that moment, they break off — temporarily — all their contacts with false gods and look upon Him only. And Allah listens to their prayer. He brings them out of the storm safely.

Then the ayah delivers its blow: **"but when He brings them safely to land, behold, they give a share of their worship to others."**

Ibn Kathir points out that this is the same picture the Qur'an draws elsewhere: *"And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon vanish from you except Him. But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away"* (17:67). And notice the word *behold* in the rendering — there they are, doing it again. Not after years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it plainly: soon after these wretched people reach the land safely, **they forget about His grace in no time** and start calling the idols His associates again. The rescue was total; the gratitude lasted the length of a walk up the beach.

Note carefully what this exposes. Their shirk — assigning to others a share of what belongs to Allah alone — was not a conclusion they had reasoned their way to. It was a habit that only survived in comfort. Danger burned it off in seconds; safety grew it back just as fast.

## ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl: the man who did not forget

Ibn Kathir places here one of the most moving reports connected to this passage — and it is the mirror image of the ayah. Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from ʿIkrimah bin Abi Jahl that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, ʿIkrimah ran away, fleeing from him. When he was on the sea, headed for Ethiopia, the ship started to rock and the crew said: **"O people, pray sincerely to your Lord alone, for no one can save us from this except Him."**

That is the exact scene of this ayah — even the sailors' own instinct, the moment sincerity becomes obvious to everyone on board. But ʿIkrimah, hearing it, drew the conclusion the ayah says most people refuse to draw. He said:

*"By Allah, if there is none who can save us on the sea except Him, then there is none who can save us on land except Him either. O Allah, I vow to You that if I come out of this, I will go and put my hand in the hand of Muhammad and I will find him kind and merciful."*

Ibn Kathir adds: **and this is what indeed did happen.**

Sit with that logic, because it is the passage's whole argument compressed into one sentence. Everyone on that ship agreed that only Allah could save them at sea. ʿIkrimah simply refused to let that truth expire when the ship docked. The One who is the only refuge in the water is the only refuge on the sand. Nothing changed about Allah when the danger passed — only about them.

And notice the second half of his vow. He did not only resolve on calling upon Allah alone; he resolved to put his hand in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, expecting to find him kind and merciful — and, Ibn Kathir tells us, that is what happened. Sincerity at sea, in his case, turned into surrender on land. That is what this passage is asking of every reader.

## The mercy hidden inside the storm

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note here that is easy to rush past. This ayah tells us that when a disbeliever regards himself as totally helpless and calls upon Allah for help in the belief that no one else can save him from the calamity, **at that moment Allah accepts the prayer of even a disbeliever** — because at that time he is a *muḍṭarr*, one driven to desperation with nowhere left to turn; and Allah has promised to accept the prayer of a *muḍṭarr*. This is given on the authority of Qurtubi.

Think about what that says about your Lord. The people in this ayah offer no guarantee of loyalty, no track record, no reason at all to be rescued. They are answered anyway, because they were desperate and they called on Him alone. The storm in this passage is not only an exposure; it is also a mercy — a moment in which Allah lets a person taste for himself that He alone answers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also anticipates an objection. Does not another ayah declare *"the prayer of the disbelievers does not but go astray"* (13:14)? The answer given is that this relates to the Hereafter, where no entreaty from them will be accepted when they appeal for mercy against the torment. Here in this world, the door is still open.

## The verdict

Ibn Kathir renders the closing ayah of the passage as the consequence of everything before it:

**"So that they become ingrate for that which We have given them, and that they take their enjoyment, but they will come to know."**

This is what all that rescuing came to: ingratitude and indulgence.

Two things are named. First, ingratitude — and what they are ungrateful *for* is specified exactly: **"that which We have given them,"** which includes, most pointedly, the rescue described in the ayah just before. The very hand that pulled them out of the water is the favour they deny. Second, *wa-li-yatamattaʿū*, **"and that they take their enjoyment"** — which lands the passage back where it began, in the amusement and play that this life was said to be. The reader who has followed the arc from the first ayah to the last finds the circle closed.

Then it ends with words that hang in the air: **"but they will come to know."** The passage opened with *if they but knew.* It closes by telling us that they will. The knowledge they refused to acquire while it could still have changed their choices will arrive on its own. What exactly they will come to know is not spelled out — which makes the warning heavier, not lighter.

## Living it

The passage does not let a believer off the hook, because the pattern it describes is not only the idolater's. It is a human reflex.

**Watch what happens to your duʿā' when the danger passes.** Ibn Kathir's question is the one to sit with: they call on Allah alone at times of calamity — so why not all the time? The test is not whether you turn to Allah in the scan results, the turbulence, the phone call at 3 a.m. Everyone does that; even the sailors on ʿIkrimah's ship knew to do that. The test is the week afterwards — whether the prayer you prayed at sea survives on land.

**Sincerity is measured after the crisis, not only in it.** Their worship in the storm was real and Allah answered it. What condemned them was that it did not outlive the danger. The one who worships Allah alone when nothing is threatening him is answering Ibn Kathir's question with his life.

**Ingratitude usually looks like forgetting, not defiance.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase is that they forget His grace *in no time*. Very few people consciously decide to be ungrateful for a rescue; they simply get absorbed again — which is precisely why the passage opens by calling this world amusement and play. The forgetting is a symptom of treating the game as the main event.

**Use the test Ibn Kathir gives.** If they but knew, they would prefer what lasts over what will pass away. So ask it of a real decision: which of these two am I actually preferring? The answer tells you what you know, whatever you say you believe. And ʿIkrimah's one line is the whole cure, portable enough to carry: if He is the only one who can save me out there, He is the only one who can save me here.
