These three ayat close Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt by answering an excuse. The Meccans were being asked to abandon their idols and believe in the Messenger ﷺ, and one of the things holding them back was fear for their lives. Ayah 67 dismantles that fear by pointing to the one place on earth where Allah had already made them safe; ayah 68 names the real wrong they were committing; and ayah 69 turns from the people making excuses to the people who push through, with a promise attached.

What holds the three together is a single movement: **a blessing they refused to read correctly (67), the crime that refusal amounts to (68), and the opposite of it — those who strive and are guided (69).**

## The excuse that ayah 67 is answering

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports (citing *Rūḥ*) that some of the disbelievers in Makkah used to put forward a particular plea. They were not claiming Islam was false. They said, in effect: we accept Islam as the true faith — but if we were converted to it and followed its tenets, we would be risking our lives against the Arab world, which is deadly against Islam. If we became Muslims, the Arabs would pounce upon us and kill us.

Read ayah 67 against that plea and it lands very differently. Allah does not argue with their reading of the political situation. He simply points at where they are standing. Ibn Kathir renders the ayah:

> *Have they not seen that We have made a secure sanctuary, while men are being snatched away from all around them?*

The picture is exact: the wider Arab world is a place where men are snatched away, and in the middle of it sits a secure sanctuary that has been placed there — the verb is *We have made* — by Allah Himself. The very danger they were pleading is precisely the danger they, uniquely, had been exempted from. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict is blunt: putting forward the risk of life as justification for non-acceptance of Islam was only a lame excuse.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also links this to what came just before in the sūrah. In the preceding verses, it says, the deeds and actions of the infidels were described as foolish and irrational: on the one hand they accept Allah as the sole Creator and master of everything, and on the other they associate their self-chiseled idols with Him. And it is not that they merely believe Him to be the sole Creator — they know well that it is only He who brings them out safely from all types of calamities. Yet after achieving deliverance, they get involved again in associating their idols with Him. Ayah 67 is one more instance of that pattern, and perhaps the most visible one, because they were living inside the evidence.

## What a *ḥaram* actually was

The word in ayah 67 is **ḥaram** — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "a peaceful sanctuary." It spells out how much this meant in practice. Allah had made the entire land of Makkah a *ḥaram*. All Arabs respected the *ḥaram*, whether they were believers or infidels; they all believed that killing was not allowed there. And the ban went further than killing and fighting: hunting and the cutting of trees were not permitted either. If any stranger entered the *ḥaram*, his life would be completely secured.

Ibn Kathir adds the social side of it. Here Allah reminds Quraysh how He blessed them by granting them access to His sanctuary, which He has made open to all men — the dweller in it and the visitor from the country are equal there — and whoever enters it is safe, because he is in a place of great security, although the Arabs of the desert round about used to ambush and raid one another and kill one another.

This is what makes the honour so striking, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words: Allah had accorded such an honour and eminence to the Makkans as is not available to any people living anywhere in the world.

Ibn Kathir points to the sūrah that says exactly this:

> *For the protection of the Quraysh. The caravans to set forth safe in winter and in summer. So let them worship the Lord of this House. Who has fed them against hunger, and has made them safe from fear.* (106:1-4)

Fed against hunger and made safe from fear — the two things human beings organise their whole lives around, handed to them; and the conclusion Allah draws from it is one line: *so let them worship the Lord of this House.*

## Believing falsehood, denying the Giver

The second half of ayah 67 asks the question the blessing demands:

> *Then do they believe in falsehood, and deny the graces of Allah?*

Ibn Kathir renders the force of it as a question with an obvious answer: is *this* the thanks they give for so immense a blessing — to associate others with Him and worship others besides Him, idols and rivals?

Notice the shape of the accusation. It is not that they lack belief; they believe intensely — in falsehood. And it is not that they fail to receive the favour; they enjoy it daily and deny its Source. Faith and ingratitude are both present, just pointed the wrong way. Ibn Kathir places beside it another ayah about the same reversal: *Have you not seen those who have changed the blessings of Allah into disbelief, and caused their people to dwell in the house of destruction?* (14:28)

He then says plainly what they should have done and what they did instead. They disbelieved in the Prophet, servant and Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when what they should have done was to worship Allah alone and not associate anything with Him, and to believe in, honour and respect the Messenger. But they rejected him and fought him, and expelled him from their midst.

And Ibn Kathir tells the end of that story, which the ayah's first listeners had not yet lived: so Allah took His blessing away from them, and killed those of them whom He killed at Badr; then His Messenger ﷺ and the believers gained the upper hand, and Allah enabled His Messenger ﷺ to conquer Makkah, and He disgraced them and humiliated them. The people who feared being snatched away if they followed him were, in the end, the ones who lost the security they were clinging to — because security was never a property of the place. It was a gift, and gifts have an Owner.

## Ayah 68: the two who are punished most severely

> *And who does more wrong than he who invents a lie against Allah or denies the truth, when it comes to him? Is there not a dwelling in Hell for the disbelievers?*

The question "who does more wrong…?" is a way of saying: no one. Ibn Kathir explains the two halves as two distinct crimes, each at the very top of the scale of punishment.

**The fabricator.** There is no one who will be more severely punished than one who tells lies about Allah and says that Allah revealed something to him at the time when Allah did not reveal anything to him, or says, "I shall reveal something like that which Allah revealed."

**The denier.** And there is no one who will be more severely punished than one who denies the truth when it comes to him. Ibn Kathir sums up the pair: the former is a fabricator, and the latter is a disbeliever.

Both are failures in the same faculty — the honest handling of what is true about Allah. One invents what He did not say; the other refuses what He did say. And note the timing built into the ayah: *when it comes to him*. This is not about someone who never heard. It is about a truth that arrived and was pushed away. Which is exactly the position of the Makkans in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's report: they accepted Islam as the true faith and still refused to follow it.

The closing line, *Is there not a dwelling in Hell for the disbelievers?*, is put as a question rather than a statement — the sort of question whose answer is meant to be admitted, not merely heard.

## Ayah 69: what it means to strive

> *As for those who strive hard for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And verily, Allah is with the doers of good.*

**Who are they?** Ibn Kathir: the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions and those who follow him, until the Day of Resurrection. The door is explicitly left open to everyone who comes after.

**What is the striving?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the definition carefully: the real meaning of *jihād* is to put in all efforts to remove the hurdles in the way of faith. Those hurdles come from two directions — those put up by the infidels, for which fighting is at the top pedestal, and those created by one's own self and by Shayṭān. There is a promise in this verse, it says, for **both** types of *jihād*. So the ayah covers the believer facing external hostility and the believer wrestling with his own self; neither is left outside the promise.

The Arabic is *jāhadū fīnā*. The renderings before us are "those who strive hard for Us" and "those who struggle in Our cause" — the striving is not merely energetic; it is *for Him*, which is what makes it count.

**What is promised?** *La-nahdiyannahum subulanā* — "We will **surely** guide them," the emphasis carried over from the Arabic. And the object is plural: *subulanā*, "Our path**s**." Ibn Kathir explains it as: *We will help them to follow Our path in this world and the Hereafter.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the promise wonderfully concrete. It means that when there is a confusion between evil and virtue, truth and false, and profit or loss, and a wise person wonders which way to adopt — on such occasions Allah guides those striving in His way to the path which is straight, righteous and without risk. In other words, He turns their hearts toward a way that may bring the divine blessing and the best results.

That is worth sitting with. The first reward named for striving is not ease, or victory, or relief. It is **clarity** — the ability to see the right move when the situation is murky. To anyone who has stood at a fork and not known which branch was the honest one, that is an enormous mercy.

## Act on what you know, and you will be given what you don't

The commentators build on this promise in one shared direction, and it is the most practical thing in the passage.

Ibn Kathir narrates that Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAbbās al-Hamdānī Abū Aḥmad — one of the people of ʿAkkā (Palestine) — who said concerning this ayah: **"Those who act upon what they know, Allah will guide them to that which they do not know."** Knowledge is not stored, it is spent; and what is spent comes back multiplied.

Ibn Kathir continues the conversation: Aḥmad bin Abū al-Ḥawārī said, "I told this to Abū Sulaymān ad-Dārānī, and he liked it," and Abū Sulaymān added a caution — that no one who is inspired to do something good should do it until he hears a report concerning that; if he hears a report, then he should go ahead and do it, and praise Allah because it was in accordance with what he himself felt. Inspiration is checked against transmitted knowledge, not substituted for it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same principle from two early authorities. Sayyidnā **Abū ad-Dardāʼ** (may Allah be pleased with him), interpreting this verse, said that the people who strive to act in accordance with their knowledge are promised in this verse that Allah will disclose to them some other areas of knowledge that they did not have before. **Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ** (may Allah have mercy on him) gave yet another interpretation, turning the sentence the other way round: *those who strive for knowledge, We make it easy for them to act.* (Maẓharī)

Put the two together and you get a wheel rather than a line. Knowledge acted on earns more knowledge; knowledge sought earns the ability to act. Whichever end you start from, the striving is what turns it.

## "And verily, Allah is with the doers of good"

The ayah — and the whole sūrah — ends on *wa inna-Llāha la-maʿa l-muḥsinīn*: "And verily, Allah is with the doers of good."

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on the sūrah with a report: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that ash-Shaʿbī said that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) said: **"Righteousness means doing good to those who ill-treat you, it does not mean doing good to those who do good to you."** Reciprocating kindness is ordinary exchange. What is being asked for here is giving good where nothing was given to you — and where, sometimes, harm was.

Set that beside the situation the sūrah has been describing — a Messenger ﷺ who was rejected, fought and expelled from among his own people — and it stops being an abstract ideal. It becomes a job description for people surrounded by hostility. And the assurance attached to it is the last word of the sūrah: Allah is with the doers of good.

## Living it

- The excuse in ayah 67 was fear of what people would do. The answer was not a guarantee of comfort but a reminder of who actually holds safety. Whatever we tell ourselves we cannot afford to obey Allah in, the honest question is the one ayah 67 asks: *have they not seen* what He has already done for them?
- Ingratitude in this passage is not rudeness; it is misdirected worship. The test of a blessing is where it sends you.
- Ayah 68 is a warning to be scrupulously careful about what we attribute to Allah — never to say "Allah says" or "Islam says" without knowing.
- Ayah 69 is the standing offer. Strive in His cause — outwardly against what obstructs the faith, inwardly against the self and Shayṭān — and act on the knowledge you already have. The guidance you are missing tends to come as the reward for the obedience you are not yet giving.

*And Allah knows best.* With this the tafsir of Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt closes — all praise and thanks are due to Allah.
